Arbitrary inferences - when someone sees a discrepancy between themselves and others and assume that this is because of them e.g 'John got the job, he's just like me I must have done something wrong and I'll never get a job' Black and white thinking - inability to see things in the grey e.g 'I didn't get the top spot so I'm a failure' Catastrophising - taking a situation too far ahead e.g 'I didn't get the top spot so I'll never get into a good university, my life will be ruined' Personalising - assuming that an event has a direct effect on you e.g 'The shop was so busy today, I must have been standin by the tills so people kept on colliding with me' Selective thinking - focusing only on things that confirm your existing beliefs e.g 'I didn't get the top spot so it must be because my revision wasn't good enough, all the other people who got in must have had your dad sit for their exams with them they must have given them answers' See page 445 of 'Living with Psychosis p.p. 12-13' and web resources below for more information on common distortions in thinking strategies https://www.beateedust.com/cognitive-distortions/

The most appropriate first line treatment is high flow oxygen. She is having an acute decompensation event due to her Crohn's disease. This is characterised by anemia, weight loss, recurrent infections and ostomy formation. Patients with this condition are likely to have iron deficiency anaemia (low ferritin, high MCV suggesting mixed/incorrectly ID'd macrocytic anaemia), which causes hypoxia. Patients may also have folate and B12 deficiency due to terminal ileum (where B12 is absorbed) or even proximal small bowel (where folate is absorbed) damage. The presence of a nasty wound and recent vomiting also contribute to her anaemia.  Treating the hypoxia with oxygen is the most appropriate first line treatment for patients with acute decompensation.  IV iron and a B12 injection may be indicated in this patient, but oxygen is the first line treatment.  Cross matched blood transfusion is only indicated if the patient is haemodynamically unstable.  Cleaning and dressing the wound and giving a tetanus booster is also indicated, but this is not a medical option.  Source: Case 11 lecture 'ABG, circulation, breathing and blood' and the SBA cases.

Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by low numbers of granulocytes on the blood count. This can be asymptomatic or present with recurrent life-threatening infections; in severe cases can be associated with0.3-0.5 haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.  Symptoms may also include fever, muscle weakness and a sore mouth or bleeding gums.  Agranulocytosis is a known ADR of clozapine. Other ADRs include cardiac toxicity (long QT and AV block), metabolic (diabetes and hyperkalaemia), CNS (confusion, seizures and priapism in men) and haematological (reduced WBC, ANC and platelets).
